notes.front: What is the TILA-RESPA Integrated Disclosure rule (TRID)?
notes.back: The rule that merged the separate Truth in Lending Act and RESPA mortgage disclosures into integrated forms.
notes.explanation: Before it, lenders gave applicants two different disclosure forms, and generally two more at or shortly before closing.
notes.source: CFPB, TILA-RESPA Integrated Disclosure: Guide to the Loan Estimate and Closing Disclosure forms (v2.1), 1. Introduction, p. 7
notes.evidence: For more than 30 years, Federal law required lenders to provide two different disclosure forms to consumers applying for a mortgage. The law also generally required two different forms at or shortly before closing on the loan.
notes.example: Like replacing two overlapping bills from two suppliers with one statement, but for a mortgage: one early estimate form and one closing form.

notes.front: Under TRID, what counts as an application?
notes.back: Submission of six items: name, income, social security number, property address, estimated property value and loan amount sought.
notes.explanation: The regulation lists the social security number for one stated purpose: obtaining a credit report.
notes.evidence: an application consists of the submission of the consumer's name, the consumer's income, the consumer's social security number to obtain a credit report, the property address, an estimate of the value of the property, and the mortgage loan amount sought.
notes.example: Like a parcel that counts as posted only once it carries every required label, but here the labels are six pieces of information.

notes.front: What is the Loan Estimate (LE)?
notes.back: The first TRID form, which helps consumers understand the key features, costs and risks of the mortgage they are applying for.
notes.explanation: It is given while the consumer is still applying, so it shows estimates rather than the final terms.
notes.source: CFPB, TILA-RESPA Integrated Disclosure: Guide to the Loan Estimate and Closing Disclosure forms (v2.1), 1. Introduction, p. 8
notes.evidence: The first new form (Loan Estimate) is designed to provide disclosures that will be helpful to consumers in understanding the key features, costs, and risks of the mortgage loan for which they are applying.
notes.example: Like a builder's written quotation before work starts, but for a mortgage, on a standard form every lender uses.

image.alt: Page 1 of the blank Loan Estimate form: a header with date issued, applicants, property, sale price, loan term, purpose, product, loan type and rate lock; then the Loan Terms table (loan amount, interest rate, monthly principal and interest, prepayment penalty, balloon payment); the Projected Payments table; and the Costs at Closing table (estimated closing costs and estimated cash to close).
image.credit: Consumer Financial Protection Bureau, TILA-RESPA Integrated Disclosure Guide to the Loan Estimate and Closing Disclosure forms, Figure 1

notes.front: What is zero tolerance in TRID's good-faith rules?
notes.back: The general rule: a closing cost is in good faith only if the amount charged does not exceed the amount originally disclosed.
notes.explanation: It is the default for every estimated closing cost; later paragraphs of the rule set out the exceptions.
notes.evidence: An estimated closing cost disclosed pursuant to paragraph (e) of this section is in good faith if the charge paid by or imposed on the consumer does not exceed the amount originally disclosed under paragraph (e)(1)(i) of this section, except as otherwise provided
notes.example: Like a fixed-price menu where the bill cannot be higher than the printed price, but for fees on a Loan Estimate.

notes.front: What is the 10 percent tolerance in TRID?
notes.back: Third-party service charges and recording fees are in good faith if their combined total exceeds the estimate by no more than 10 per cent.
notes.explanation: The test compares aggregate amounts, so the category is measured as a whole rather than fee by fee.
notes.evidence: The aggregate amount of charges for third-party services and recording fees paid by or imposed on the consumer does not exceed the aggregate amount of such charges disclosed under paragraph (e)(1)(i) of this section by more than 10 percent
notes.example: Like a household budget line for "repairs" that may run 10 per cent over in total, even if one repair costs double.

notes.front: What is a changed circumstance under TRID?
notes.back: An event or information, specific to the consumer or transaction or beyond anyone's control, that can justify revising estimated charges upward.
notes.explanation: For the 10 per cent category it matters only if it pushes the combined charges up by more than 10 per cent.
notes.evidence: Changed circumstances cause the estimated charges to increase or, in the case of estimated charges identified in paragraph (e)(3)(ii) of this section, cause the aggregate amount of such charges to increase by more than 10 percent.
notes.example: Like a fixed quote for a decorator that can be reopened if the room turns out to be twice the size you said, but for mortgage fees.

notes.front: What is a rate lock agreement?
notes.back: An arrangement that sets the interest rate for a period of time, typically 30, 45 or 60 days, sometimes longer.
notes.explanation: An unlocked rate is "floating": it can go up or down, and mortgage rates can change daily or even hourly.
notes.source: CFPB, Your home loan toolkit, "Rate lock", p. 14
notes.evidence: Your Loan Estimate could show a rate that has been “locked” or a rate that is “floating,” which means it can go up or down. Mortgage interest rates change daily, sometimes hourly. A rate lock sets your interest rate for a period of time.
notes.example: Like reserving a hotel room at today's price for a set number of weeks, but for a mortgage interest rate.

notes.front: What is the Closing Disclosure (CD)?
notes.back: The TRID form that states the final loan terms and closing costs.
notes.explanation: The form itself tells the consumer to compare it with the Loan Estimate received earlier.
notes.evidence: This form is a statement of final loan terms and closing costs. Compare this document with your Loan Estimate.
notes.example: Like the final invoice that follows a quotation, but for a mortgage, laid out so it can be checked line by line against the Loan Estimate.

image.alt: Page 1 of the blank Closing Disclosure form: closing information, transaction information and loan information at the top; then the Loan Terms table, the Projected Payments table, and the Costs at Closing table showing closing costs and cash to close.
image.credit: Consumer Financial Protection Bureau, TILA-RESPA Integrated Disclosure Guide to the Loan Estimate and Closing Disclosure forms, Figure 28

notes.front: What is Your home loan toolkit?
notes.back: A step-by-step booklet from the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau for people buying a home.
notes.explanation: It says it is meant to help readers make better choices along the path to owning a home.
notes.source: CFPB, Your home loan toolkit, "How can this toolkit help you?", p. 2
notes.evidence: This booklet is a toolkit that can help you make better choices along your path to owning a home.
notes.example: Like a driving-test workbook, but for choosing and closing on a mortgage.

notes.front: What is cash to close?
notes.back: The total cash or other funds the consumer must provide at consummation.
notes.explanation: The Loan Estimate itemises it into component amounts in a table headed "Calculating Cash to Close".
notes.evidence: under the heading “Calculating Cash to Close,” the total amount of cash or other funds that must be provided by the consumer at consummation, with an itemization of that amount into the following component amounts:
notes.example: Like the amount due at the till after deposits and discounts, but for the closing of a home loan.

notes.front: Which transactions require a Loan Estimate?
notes.back: Closed-end consumer credit secured by real property or a cooperative unit, other than a reverse mortgage.
notes.explanation: The creditor must give good-faith estimates of the Loan Estimate disclosures for these loans.
notes.evidence: In a closed-end consumer credit transaction secured by real property or a cooperative unit, other than a reverse mortgage subject to § 1026.33, the creditor shall provide the consumer with good faith estimates of the disclosures in § 1026.37.

notes.front: TRID's early disclosure rule covers closed-end loans secured by real property or a cooperative unit, other than {{c1::reverse mortgages}}.
notes.explanation: The official interpretation repeats the carve-out when it describes the early disclosure requirement.
notes.evidence: requires early disclosure of credit terms in closed-end credit transactions that are secured by real property or a cooperative unit, other than reverse mortgages.

notes.front: Which of these loans must come with a Loan Estimate?
notes.back: B) A closed-end purchase loan secured by a house.
notes.explanation: Only closed-end credit secured by real property or a cooperative unit is covered, and reverse mortgages are carved out.
notes.evidence: In a closed-end consumer credit transaction secured by real property or a cooperative unit, other than a reverse mortgage subject to § 1026.33
notes.choices:
A) A reverse mortgage for a 70-year-old homeowner
B) A closed-end purchase loan secured by a house
C) An unsecured personal loan used for furniture
notes.choicesExplained: A: reverse mortgages are expressly excluded from this rule. C: the rule covers only credit secured by real property or a cooperative unit.

notes.front: In a TRID application, the consumer's social security number is collected {{c1::to obtain a credit report}}.
notes.explanation: It is one of the six items that together make up an application for these loans.
notes.evidence: the consumer's social security number to obtain a credit report

notes.front: A TRID application includes an estimate of {{c1::the value of the property}}.
notes.explanation: The item is an estimate of value, supplied by the consumer as part of the application.
notes.evidence: the property address, an estimate of the value of the property, and the mortgage loan amount sought.

notes.front: A TRID application includes the {{c1::mortgage loan amount sought}}.
notes.explanation: It is the last of the six listed items; once all six are submitted the consumer has applied.
notes.evidence: an estimate of the value of the property, and the mortgage loan amount sought.

notes.front: Besides the social security number, which two personal details of the consumer are part of a TRID application?
notes.back: Name and income.
notes.explanation: The other three items describe the property and the loan rather than the person.
notes.evidence: an application consists of the submission of the consumer's name, the consumer's income, the consumer's social security number

notes.front: A borrower gives a lender her name, income, social security number, the address of the flat she wants and its estimated value, but has not said how much she wants to borrow. Has she made a TRID application?
notes.back: B) No: the loan amount sought is still missing.
notes.explanation: All six listed items make up an application, and the loan amount is one of them.
notes.evidence: an application consists of the submission of the consumer's name, the consumer's income, the consumer's social security number to obtain a credit report, the property address, an estimate of the value of the property, and the mortgage loan amount sought.
notes.choices:
A) Yes: five of the six items are enough
B) No: the loan amount sought is still missing
C) No: she must also provide pay slips
notes.choicesExplained: A: the definition lists six items, not a majority of them. C: documents such as pay slips are not among the six items.

notes.front: The creditor must deliver or mail the Loan Estimate no later than the {{c1::third}} business day after it receives the application.
notes.explanation: The clock runs from the creditor's receipt of the application, and mailing on time is enough.
notes.evidence: The creditor shall deliver or place in the mail the disclosures required under paragraph (e)(1)(i) of this section not later than the third business day after the creditor receives the consumer's application

notes.front: If a mortgage broker receives the application, who may provide the Loan Estimate?
notes.back: Either the creditor or the mortgage broker.
notes.explanation: The rule places the duty on either party; it does not require both to send one.
notes.evidence: If a mortgage broker receives a consumer's application, either the creditor or the mortgage broker shall provide a consumer with the disclosures required under paragraph (e)(1)(i) of this section

notes.front: A creditor receives a complete application on a Tuesday. Its offices are open every weekday and there is no holiday that week. What is the latest day it can put the Loan Estimate in the post?
notes.back: C) Friday
notes.explanation: The deadline is the third business day after receipt, and posting by then satisfies it.
notes.evidence: not later than the third business day after the creditor receives the consumer's application
notes.choices:
A) Wednesday
B) Thursday
C) Friday
D) The following Tuesday
notes.choicesExplained: A and B: these are earlier than required, not the latest day. D: that is well past the third business day after Tuesday.

notes.front: The Loan Estimate must be delivered or mailed no later than the {{c1::seventh}} business day before consummation.
notes.explanation: This second deadline counts back from consummation rather than forward from the application.
notes.evidence: the creditor shall deliver or place in the mail the disclosures required under paragraph (e)(1)(i) of this section not later than the seventh business day before consummation of the transaction.

notes.front: When does the seven-business-day waiting period after a Loan Estimate start?
notes.back: When the creditor delivers it or puts it in the post, not when the consumer receives it.
notes.explanation: Receipt rules do not delay this period; only delivery or mailing counts.
notes.evidence: The seven-business-day waiting period begins when the creditor delivers the disclosures or places them in the mail, not when the consumer receives or is considered to have received the disclosures.

notes.front: Is Saturday a business day when counting the seven-business-day waiting period before consummation?
notes.back: Yes.
notes.explanation: This waiting period uses the calendar-based definition of business day, unlike the three-day delivery deadline.
notes.evidence: for the purposes of § 1026.19(e)(1)(iii)(B), Saturday is a business day, pursuant to § 1026.2(a)(6).

notes.front: A creditor hands over the Loan Estimate on a Wednesday. There are no public holidays in the next fortnight. What is the earliest day consummation may take place?
notes.back: B) Thursday of the following week
notes.explanation: Counting Saturday as a business day, the seventh business day after Wednesday is the next Thursday.
notes.evidence: for the purposes of § 1026.19(e)(1)(iii)(B), Saturday is a business day, pursuant to § 1026.2(a)(6).
notes.choices:
A) The following Monday
B) Thursday of the following week
C) Friday of the following week
D) Wednesday two weeks later
notes.choicesExplained: A: only four business days (Thursday, Friday, Saturday and Monday) will have passed. C: that ignores Saturday, which counts as a business day here. D: that is later than necessary.

notes.front: Before what two events may no one charge a fee in connection with an application?
notes.back: The consumer receiving the Loan Estimate, and the consumer indicating an intent to proceed.
notes.explanation: The ban covers the creditor and any other person, such as a broker.
notes.evidence: neither a creditor nor any other person may impose a fee on a consumer in connection with the consumer's application for a mortgage transaction subject to paragraph (e)(1)(i) of this section before the consumer has received the disclosures required under paragraph (e)(1)(i) of this section and indicated to the creditor an intent to proceed

notes.front: Which fee may be charged before the consumer receives the Loan Estimate?
notes.back: A bona fide and reasonable fee for obtaining the consumer's credit report.
notes.explanation: It is the only exception to the ban on up-front fees.
notes.evidence: A creditor or other person may impose a bona fide and reasonable fee for obtaining the consumer's credit report before the consumer has received the disclosures

notes.front: May a creditor require documents verifying the consumer's information before providing the Loan Estimate?
notes.back: No.
notes.explanation: The rule forbids requiring verification documents until after the Loan Estimate has been provided.
notes.evidence: The creditor or other person shall not require a consumer to submit documents verifying information related to the consumer's application before providing the disclosures

notes.front: A loan officer asks an applicant for a $500 appraisal fee on the day of application, before any Loan Estimate is sent. Is this allowed?
notes.back: C) No: no fee except a credit report fee may be charged before the consumer receives the Loan Estimate and indicates intent to proceed.
notes.explanation: Only a bona fide and reasonable credit report fee escapes the up-front fee ban.
notes.evidence: A creditor or other person may impose a bona fide and reasonable fee for obtaining the consumer's credit report before the consumer has received the disclosures
notes.choices:
A) Yes, if the fee is refundable
B) Yes, because an appraisal is a third-party service
C) No: no fee except a credit report fee may be charged before the consumer receives the Loan Estimate and indicates intent to proceed
notes.choicesExplained: A: the rule makes no exception for refundable fees. B: third-party fees are not exempt; only the credit report fee is.

notes.front: Under what heading does the Loan Estimate show the loan amount, interest rate and monthly principal and interest?
notes.back: Loan Terms.
notes.explanation: The regulation requires a separate table under that heading on the form.
notes.evidence: A separate table under the heading “Loan Terms” that contains the following information

notes.front: What does the Projected Payments table on the Loan Estimate itemise?
notes.back: Each periodic payment or range of payments, with estimated taxes, insurance and assessments and the escrow payments.
notes.explanation: So the table covers more than principal and interest.
notes.evidence: an itemization of each separate periodic payment or range of payments, together with an estimate of taxes, insurance, and assessments and the payments to be made with escrow account funds.

notes.front: Which two amounts appear in the Costs at Closing table on page 1 of the Loan Estimate?
notes.back: Closing Costs and Cash to Close.
notes.explanation: The regulation labels the two amounts with exactly those words.
notes.evidence: In a separate table, under the heading “Costs at Closing”:

notes.front: What does the "Rate Lock" field on the Loan Estimate state?
notes.back: Whether the disclosed interest rate is locked for a specific period of time.
notes.explanation: It tells the consumer whether the rate shown is fixed for a period or may still move.
notes.evidence: A statement of whether the interest rate disclosed pursuant to paragraph (b)(2) of this section is locked for a specific period of time, labeled “Rate Lock.”

notes.front: On page 1 of the Loan Estimate shown, in which table would a consumer find whether the loan has a balloon payment?
notes.back: Loan Terms.
notes.explanation: The Loan Terms table asks whether the loan has features such as a prepayment penalty or balloon payment.
notes.source: 12 CFR 1026.37(b) (Regulation Z); Figure 1 of the CFPB guide to the forms
notes.evidence: A separate table under the heading “Loan Terms” that contains the following information

image.alt: Page 1 of the blank Loan Estimate form: a header with date issued, applicants, property, sale price, loan term, purpose, product, loan type and rate lock; the Loan Terms table with loan amount, interest rate, monthly principal and interest, and, under "Does the loan have these features?", prepayment penalty and balloon payment; the Projected Payments table; and the Costs at Closing table.
image.credit: Consumer Financial Protection Bureau, TILA-RESPA Integrated Disclosure Guide to the Loan Estimate and Closing Disclosure forms, Figure 1

notes.front: If the consumer indicates intent to proceed more than {{c1::10}} business days after the Loan Estimate is provided, the creditor may use a revised estimate.
notes.explanation: The creditor may also set a longer offer period; the trigger is then that longer period.
notes.evidence: The consumer indicates an intent to proceed with the transaction more than 10 business days, or more than any additional number of days specified by the creditor before the offer expires

notes.front: What justification does a creditor need to revise estimates after the Loan Estimate has expired?
notes.back: None beyond the lapse of 10 business days.
notes.explanation: Unlike a changed circumstance, expiry needs no event: time passing is enough.
notes.evidence: Section 1026.19(e)(3)(iv)(E) requires no justification for the change to the original estimate other than the lapse of 10 business days.

notes.front: A consumer receives a Loan Estimate, then waits 14 business days before telling the creditor she wants to go ahead. The creditor set no longer offer period. What may the creditor do?
notes.back: A) Issue revised estimates and measure good faith against them.
notes.explanation: Intent to proceed came more than 10 business days after the estimate was provided, so the original estimate has expired.
notes.evidence: The consumer indicates an intent to proceed with the transaction more than 10 business days
notes.choices:
A) Issue revised estimates and measure good faith against them
B) Nothing: the original estimates bind it until closing
C) Revise only if a changed circumstance also occurs
notes.choicesExplained: B: expiry releases the creditor from the original estimates. C: expiry is a separate ground and needs no other event.

notes.front: A written estimate given before the Loan Estimate must say at the top: "Your actual rate, payment, and costs could be higher. {{c1::Get an official Loan Estimate before choosing a loan.}}"
notes.explanation: The statement must be clear and conspicuous, in at least 12-point font, on the first page.
notes.evidence: shall clearly and conspicuously state at the top of the front of the first page of the estimate in a font size that is no smaller than 12-point font: “Your actual rate, payment, and costs could be higher. Get an official Loan Estimate before choosing a loan.”

notes.front: Which tolerance category generally applies to fees paid to the creditor?
notes.back: Zero tolerance.
notes.explanation: The interpretation lists them first among charges generally held to the amount originally disclosed.
notes.evidence: i. Fees paid to the creditor.

notes.front: Which tolerance category generally applies to fees paid to a mortgage broker?
notes.back: Zero tolerance.
notes.explanation: Broker fees sit in the same list as the creditor's own fees.
notes.evidence: ii. Fees paid to a mortgage broker.

notes.front: Which tolerance category generally applies to fees paid to an affiliate of the creditor or broker?
notes.back: Zero tolerance.
notes.explanation: Paying an affiliate does not move a fee out of the strictest category.
notes.evidence: iii. Fees paid to an affiliate of the creditor or a mortgage broker.

notes.front: When is a fee paid to an unaffiliated third party subject to zero tolerance?
notes.back: When the creditor did not permit the consumer to shop for that settlement service provider.
notes.explanation: The provider is unaffiliated, yet without shopping the fee is still held to the amount originally disclosed.
notes.evidence: iv. Fees paid to an unaffiliated third party if the creditor did not permit the consumer to shop for a third party service provider for a settlement service.

notes.front: Which tolerance category generally applies to transfer taxes?
notes.back: Zero tolerance.
notes.explanation: An increase above the original estimate breaches the general good-faith limit, even though a government imposes the tax.
notes.evidence: the increase in transfer taxes paid by the consumer also exceeds the amount originally disclosed under § 1026.19(e)(1)(i) above the limitations prescribed by § 1026.19(e)(3)(i).

notes.front: A Loan Estimate shows a $450 underwriting fee payable to the creditor. At closing the creditor charges $475 and no reason for revision applies. How is the $25 increase treated?
notes.back: B) It exceeds zero tolerance, so the creditor must refund it.
notes.explanation: Creditor fees may not rise above the amount originally disclosed.
notes.evidence: i. Fees paid to the creditor.
notes.choices:
A) It is fine: it is under 10 per cent
B) It exceeds zero tolerance, so the creditor must refund it
C) It is fine: underwriting fees have no limit
notes.choicesExplained: A: the 10 per cent category is for third-party services and recording fees, not creditor fees. C: no-limit charges are things like prepaid interest and escrow amounts, not creditor fees.

notes.front: For a third-party charge to fall in the 10 percent tolerance, to whom must it not be paid?
notes.back: The creditor or an affiliate of the creditor.
notes.explanation: A charge paid to the creditor or its affiliate stays in zero tolerance instead.
notes.evidence: The charge for the third-party service is not paid to the creditor or an affiliate of the creditor; and

notes.front: What must the creditor permit for a third-party charge to fall in the 10 percent tolerance?
notes.back: It must permit the consumer to shop for that third-party service.
notes.explanation: Shopping means the consumer may select the provider, subject to reasonable requirements.
notes.evidence: A creditor permits a consumer to shop for a settlement service if the creditor permits the consumer to select the provider of that service, subject to reasonable requirements.

notes.front: Besides third-party service charges, which charge falls in the 10 percent tolerance?
notes.back: Recording fees.
notes.explanation: Recording fees are paid to the government office that records the documents, not to a third-party provider.
notes.evidence: Recording fees are not charges for third-party services because recording fees are paid to the applicable government entity where the documents related to the mortgage transaction are recorded

notes.front: In the 10 percent tolerance, what if one charge rises by more than 10 per cent but the category total does not?
notes.back: The charge is still in good faith; only the total of the category is tested.
notes.explanation: This holds even if a charge was left off the Loan Estimate and then imposed at consummation.
notes.evidence: depends on whether the sum of all charges subject to § 1026.19(e)(3)(ii) increases by more than 10 percent, regardless of whether a particular charge increases by more than 10 percent. This is true even if an individual charge was omitted from the estimate

notes.front: If the consumer may shop for a settlement service, what must the creditor give?
notes.back: A written list of available providers, with at least one per service, saying the consumer may choose another.
notes.explanation: It is given separately from the Loan Estimate but on the same timetable.
notes.evidence: The creditor must identify at least one available provider for each settlement service for which the consumer is permitted to shop. The creditor shall provide this written list of settlement service providers separately from the disclosures required by paragraph (e)(1)(i) of this section but in accordance with the timing requirements

notes.front: Charges in the 10 percent category were estimated at $1,000 in total. At closing the pest inspection costs double its estimate, but the category total is $1,070. Are these charges in good faith?
notes.back: A) Yes: the category total rose by only 7 per cent.
notes.explanation: The test is whether the sum of all charges in the category rose by more than 10 per cent.
notes.evidence: regardless of whether a particular charge increases by more than 10 percent.
notes.choices:
A) Yes: the category total rose by only 7 per cent
B) No: one charge rose by 100 per cent
C) No: any increase in a third-party charge must be refunded
notes.choicesExplained: B: individual charges are not tested one by one. C: that describes zero tolerance, not the 10 percent category.

notes.front: Which TRID tolerance category covers prepaid interest?
notes.back: No tolerance limit: it only has to be based on the best information reasonably available.
notes.explanation: It appears first in the list of charges that may vary without breaching good faith.
notes.evidence: An estimate of any of the charges specified in this paragraph (e)(3)(iii) is in good faith if it is consistent with the best information reasonably available

notes.front: Property {{c1::insurance premiums}} are among the charges with no tolerance limit under TRID.
notes.explanation: Like prepaid interest, they need only be estimated on the best information reasonably available.
notes.evidence: Estimates of prepaid interest, property insurance premiums, and amounts placed into an escrow, impound, reserve or similar account must be consistent with the best information reasonably available

notes.front: What tolerance applies to amounts placed into an escrow account at closing?
notes.back: No tolerance limit, as long as the estimate used the best information reasonably available.
notes.explanation: Escrow deposits are listed with prepaid interest and property insurance premiums.
notes.evidence: Estimates of prepaid interest, property insurance premiums, and amounts placed into an escrow, impound, reserve or similar account must be consistent with the best information reasonably available

notes.front: Which tolerance applies to a required service when the consumer picks a provider not on the creditor's list?
notes.back: No tolerance limit.
notes.explanation: The actual fees need not be compared with the original estimates in that case.
notes.evidence: the consumer chooses a service provider that is not on that list to perform that service, then the actual amounts of such fees need not be compared to the original estimates

notes.front: What are two kinds of charge in (e)(3)(iii)(E) that have no tolerance limit?
notes.back: Property taxes, and charges for third-party services the creditor does not require.
notes.explanation: The regulation groups them together as one item of the no-limit list.
notes.evidence: (E) Property taxes and other charges paid for third-party services not required by the creditor.

notes.front: The creditor lets the borrower shop for a title service. She ignores its list and hires her cousin's firm, whose fee ends up well above the estimate. Which tolerance applies to that fee?
notes.back: C) No tolerance limit.
notes.explanation: A required service from a provider the consumer chose off the list is not compared with the estimate.
notes.evidence: (D) Charges paid to third-party service providers selected by the consumer consistent with paragraph (e)(1)(vi)(A) of this section that are not on the list provided
notes.choices:
A) Zero tolerance
B) 10 percent tolerance
C) No tolerance limit
notes.choicesExplained: A: zero tolerance would apply if she had not been allowed to shop. B: the 10 percent category applies when she uses a provider from the creditor's list.

notes.front: If a consumer pays more than the tolerance allows, the creditor cures it by refunding the excess no later than {{c1::60}} days after consummation.
notes.explanation: It must also deliver or post a corrected Closing Disclosure showing the refund within the same period.
notes.evidence: the creditor complies with paragraph (e)(1)(i) of this section if the creditor refunds the excess to the consumer no later than 60 days after consummation

notes.front: Besides the refund, what must a creditor send within 60 days of consummation to cure a tolerance breach?
notes.back: Corrected disclosures that reflect the refund.
notes.explanation: The refund cures the Loan Estimate breach; the corrected disclosure cures the Closing Disclosure.
notes.evidence: the creditor complies with paragraph (f)(1)(i) of this section if the creditor delivers or places in the mail corrected disclosures that reflect such refund no later than 60 days after consummation.

notes.front: Three weeks after closing, a lender finds it charged $120 more in creditor fees than its Loan Estimate allowed. What should it do?
notes.back: B) Refund the $120 and send corrected disclosures, both within 60 days of consummation.
notes.explanation: The rule lets the creditor cure the excess after closing if it acts within 60 days.
notes.evidence: if the creditor refunds the excess to the consumer no later than 60 days after consummation
notes.choices:
A) Nothing: once the loan has closed, it is too late
B) Refund the $120 and send corrected disclosures, both within 60 days of consummation
C) Refund only the part above 10 per cent
notes.choicesExplained: A: the rule allows a cure for 60 days after consummation. C: creditor fees are zero tolerance, so the whole excess is refunded.

notes.front: Which kind of event beyond anyone's control counts as a changed circumstance?
notes.back: An extraordinary event beyond the control of any interested party.
notes.explanation: The interpretation gives a war or a natural disaster as examples.
notes.evidence: A changed circumstance may be an extraordinary event beyond the control of any interested party. For example, a war or a natural disaster would be an extraordinary event beyond the control of an interested party.

notes.front: When does information the creditor relied on for the Loan Estimate become a changed circumstance?
notes.back: When it was inaccurate, or changed after the disclosures were provided.
notes.explanation: The information must be specific to the consumer or the transaction.
notes.evidence: (2) Information specific to the consumer or transaction that the creditor relied upon when providing the disclosures required under paragraph (e)(1)(i) of this section and that was inaccurate or changed after the disclosures were provided; or

notes.front: Can information the creditor did not rely on for the original Loan Estimate be a changed circumstance?
notes.back: Yes, if it is new information specific to the consumer or transaction.
notes.explanation: This third limb covers facts that surface only after the estimate was issued.
notes.evidence: (3) New information specific to the consumer or transaction that the creditor did not rely on when providing the original disclosures

notes.front: After a changed circumstance, how far may a revised charge rise for good-faith purposes?
notes.back: Only as far as the changed circumstance actually increased that charge.
notes.explanation: Other charges cannot be raised on the back of an unrelated event.
notes.evidence: based on the increased charges reflected on revised disclosures only to the extent that the reason for revision, as identified in § 1026.19(e)(3)(iv)(A) through (F), actually increased the particular charge.

notes.front: After the Loan Estimate is issued, the title insurer the creditor had priced goes out of business during underwriting, and the replacement costs more. Is this a changed circumstance?
notes.back: A) Yes: an unexpected event specific to the transaction.
notes.explanation: Unexpected events specific to the consumer or transaction qualify, and the interpretation uses a failed title insurer as its example.
notes.evidence: if the creditor provided an estimate of title insurance on the disclosures required under § 1026.19(e)(1)(i), but the title insurer goes out of business during underwriting, then this unexpected event specific to the transaction is a changed circumstance.
notes.choices:
A) Yes: an unexpected event specific to the transaction
B) No: only wars and natural disasters count
C) No: third-party costs can never be revised
notes.choicesExplained: B: those are examples of extraordinary events, but unexpected events specific to the transaction also count. C: third-party charges can be revised for a changed circumstance.

notes.front: When does a changed circumstance affecting eligibility allow a revised estimate?
notes.back: When it affects the consumer's creditworthiness or the value of the security, making the consumer ineligible for an estimated charge.
notes.explanation: It is a separate ground from a changed circumstance that simply raises settlement charges.
notes.evidence: The consumer is ineligible for an estimated charge previously disclosed because a changed circumstance, as defined under paragraph (e)(3)(iv)(A) of this section, affected the consumer's creditworthiness or the value of the security for the loan.

notes.front: Can a consumer's own request justify a revised Loan Estimate?
notes.back: Yes: revisions the consumer requests to the credit terms or the settlement that increase a charge.
notes.explanation: It is one of the six listed reasons for using a revised estimate.
notes.evidence: The consumer requests revisions to the credit terms or the settlement that cause an estimated charge to increase.

notes.front: When may a creditor revise estimates because settlement of a new-construction loan is delayed?
notes.back: If settlement is expected over 60 days after the Loan Estimate, which clearly warned that revised disclosures may come until 60 days before consummation.
notes.explanation: Without that warning on the original Loan Estimate this ground is not available, because new-construction settlements often run late and the consumer must be told costs may be revised.
notes.evidence: where the creditor reasonably expects that settlement will occur more than 60 days after the disclosures required under paragraph (e)(1)(i) of this section are provided

notes.front: Which of these lets a creditor use a revised Loan Estimate for good-faith purposes?
notes.back: B) The borrower asks to switch to a larger loan, which raises the fees.
notes.explanation: A consumer-requested revision that increases a charge is one of the listed reasons.
notes.evidence: The consumer requests revisions to the credit terms or the settlement that cause an estimated charge to increase.
notes.choices:
A) The creditor raises its fees for all customers
B) The borrower asks to switch to a larger loan, which raises the fees
C) The creditor under-estimated a fee by mistake
notes.choicesExplained: A: a general price rise is not specific to the consumer or transaction. C: a creditor's own error is not among the listed reasons for revision.

notes.front: A revised Loan Estimate must be provided within {{c1::three}} business days of receiving information sufficient to establish a reason for revision.
notes.explanation: The three days run from when the creditor has sufficient information, not from when the event happened.
notes.evidence: reflecting the revised estimate within three business days of receiving information sufficient to establish that one of the reasons for revision provided under paragraphs (e)(3)(iv)(A) through (F) of this section applies.

notes.front: On Monday a creditor learns that the borrower's income was overstated, which raises a fee. Its offices open every weekday. By when must it provide the revised Loan Estimate to rely on it?
notes.back: A) Thursday
notes.explanation: The revised estimate is due within three business days of receiving sufficient information.
notes.evidence: within three business days of receiving information sufficient to establish that one of the reasons for revision
notes.choices:
A) Thursday
B) The following Monday
C) Any time before closing
notes.choicesExplained: B: that is five business days later. C: the three-business-day limit applies, not just "before closing".

notes.front: May a creditor send a revised Loan Estimate on or after the day it provides the Closing Disclosure?
notes.back: No.
notes.explanation: From that day on, changes go on a corrected Closing Disclosure instead.
notes.evidence: The creditor shall not provide a revised version of the disclosures required under paragraph (e)(1)(i) of this section on or after the date on which the creditor provides the disclosures required under paragraph (f)(1)(i) of this section.

notes.front: The consumer must receive any revised Loan Estimate no later than {{c1::four}} business days before consummation.
notes.explanation: If it is not handed over in person, receipt is presumed three business days after delivery or mailing.
notes.evidence: The consumer must receive any revised version of the disclosures required under paragraph (e)(1)(i) of this section not later than four business days prior to consummation.

notes.front: A creditor gave the Closing Disclosure on Tuesday. On Wednesday the borrower asks for a change that raises a fee. How should the creditor disclose the revised fee?
notes.back: C) On a corrected Closing Disclosure
notes.explanation: A revised Loan Estimate may not be provided on or after the date the Closing Disclosure was provided.
notes.evidence: The creditor shall not provide a revised version of the disclosures required under paragraph (e)(1)(i) of this section on or after the date on which the creditor provides the disclosures
notes.choices:
A) On a revised Loan Estimate
B) On both a revised Loan Estimate and a corrected Closing Disclosure
C) On a corrected Closing Disclosure
notes.choicesExplained: A and B: once the Closing Disclosure has been provided, a revised Loan Estimate is not allowed.

notes.front: When an unlocked rate is later locked, what must the creditor send, and when?
notes.back: A revised Loan Estimate, no later than three business days after the lock.
notes.explanation: It shows the locked rate, points, lender credits and other rate-dependent charges and terms.
notes.evidence: No later than three business days after the date the interest rate is locked, the creditor shall provide a revised version of the disclosures required under paragraph (e)(1)(i) of this section to the consumer with the revised interest rate

notes.front: Why may points change after the Loan Estimate without breaching good faith?
notes.back: Because the interest rate was not locked when the Loan Estimate was provided.
notes.explanation: Points and lender credits depend on the rate, so they may move until it is locked.
notes.evidence: The points or lender credits change because the interest rate was not locked when the disclosures required under paragraph (e)(1)(i) of this section were provided.

notes.front: A borrower receives a Loan Estimate with a floating rate and locks the rate a week later. What must the creditor do?
notes.back: B) Provide a revised Loan Estimate within three business days of the lock.
notes.explanation: Locking the rate is the trigger for a revised estimate showing rate-dependent charges.
notes.evidence: no later than three business days after the date the interest rate is subsequently locked, § 1026.19(e)(3)(iv)(D) requires the creditor to provide a revised version of the disclosures
notes.choices:
A) Nothing until the Closing Disclosure
B) Provide a revised Loan Estimate within three business days of the lock
C) Provide a revised Loan Estimate only if the rate went up
notes.choicesExplained: A: the rule requires a revised Loan Estimate after the lock. C: the duty applies whichever way the rate moved.

notes.front: In a transaction that required a Loan Estimate, what must the Closing Disclosure reflect?
notes.back: The actual terms of the transaction.
notes.explanation: The Loan Estimate gave good-faith estimates; the Closing Disclosure replaces them with the real figures.
notes.evidence: the creditor shall provide the consumer with the disclosures required under § 1026.38 reflecting the actual terms of the transaction.

notes.front: May a creditor or servicer charge a fee for preparing or delivering the Closing Disclosure?
notes.back: No.
notes.explanation: The ban covers fees charged as part of settlement costs or otherwise.
notes.evidence: No fee may be imposed on any person, as a part of settlement costs or otherwise, by a creditor or by a servicer

notes.front: The consumer must receive the Closing Disclosure no later than {{c1::three}} business days before consummation.
notes.explanation: The rule is about receipt, not mailing, so posting it on time is not always enough.
notes.evidence: the creditor shall ensure that the consumer receives the disclosures required under paragraph (f)(1)(i) of this section no later than three business days before consummation.

notes.front: For the Closing Disclosure's three-day rule, what is a business day?
notes.back: Every calendar day except Sundays and legal public holidays.
notes.explanation: This is the precise definition, which differs from the offices-open definition used for the three-day Loan Estimate deadline.
notes.evidence: the term “business day” means all calendar days except Sundays and legal public holidays referred to in § 1026.2(a)(6).

notes.front: For a timeshare loan, when must the consumer receive the Closing Disclosure?
notes.back: No later than consummation.
notes.explanation: The three-business-day advance rule does not apply to timeshares.
notes.evidence: For transactions secured by a consumer's interest in a timeshare plan described in 11 U.S.C. 101(53D), the creditor shall ensure that the consumer receives the disclosures required under paragraph (f)(1)(i) of this section no later than consummation.

notes.front: Closing is set for a Friday, with no holidays that week. The creditor will hand the Closing Disclosure to the borrower in person. What is the latest day it can do so?
notes.back: B) Tuesday
notes.explanation: Counting back three business days from Friday gives Tuesday, and hand delivery means receipt that day.
notes.evidence: the creditor shall ensure that the consumer receives the disclosures required under paragraph (f)(1)(i) of this section no later than three business days before consummation.
notes.choices:
A) Monday
B) Tuesday
C) Wednesday
D) Thursday
notes.choicesExplained: A: Monday works but is not the latest day. C and D: fewer than three business days would remain before closing.

notes.front: If the Closing Disclosure is posted rather than handed over, when is the consumer considered to have received it?
notes.back: Three business days after it is delivered or placed in the post.
notes.explanation: The three-day waiting period then runs from that presumed receipt, not from posting.
notes.evidence: If any disclosures required under paragraph (f)(1)(i) of this section are not provided to the consumer in person, the consumer is considered to have received the disclosures three business days after they are delivered or placed in the mail.

notes.front: A creditor posts the Closing Disclosure on a Monday, with no holidays that week. On which day is the borrower considered to have received it?
notes.back: C) Thursday
notes.explanation: Posted disclosures are presumed received three business days after mailing.
notes.evidence: the consumer is considered to have received the disclosures three business days after they are delivered or placed in the mail.
notes.choices:
A) Monday
B) Tuesday
C) Thursday
D) The following Monday
notes.choicesExplained: A: receipt on the day of posting applies only to in-person delivery. B: one day is not enough under the rule. D: that is later than the presumption.

notes.front: Which change to the annual percentage rate on the Closing Disclosure starts a new three-business-day waiting period?
notes.back: The annual percentage rate becoming inaccurate.
notes.explanation: Accuracy is measured under the regulation's own tolerance rules for the annual percentage rate.
notes.evidence: (A) The annual percentage rate disclosed under § 1026.38(o)(4) becomes inaccurate, as defined in § 1026.22.

notes.front: Which change to the kind of loan starts a new three-business-day Closing Disclosure waiting period?
notes.back: A change in the loan product.
notes.explanation: The product description disclosed on the form would otherwise become wrong.
notes.evidence: (B) The loan product is changed, causing the information disclosed under § 1026.38(a)(5)(iii) to become inaccurate.

notes.front: Which added loan feature starts a new three-business-day Closing Disclosure waiting period?
notes.back: A prepayment penalty.
notes.explanation: Adding one makes the form's prepayment penalty statement inaccurate.
notes.evidence: (C) A prepayment penalty is added, causing the statement regarding a prepayment penalty required under § 1026.38(b) to become inaccurate.

notes.front: If the Closing Disclosure becomes inaccurate in some other way, when must the consumer get corrected disclosures?
notes.back: At or before consummation.
notes.explanation: Only the three listed changes restart the waiting period.
notes.evidence: the creditor shall provide corrected disclosures reflecting any changed terms to the consumer so that the consumer receives the corrected disclosures at or before consummation.

notes.front: Two days before closing, which of these changes means the borrower must receive a corrected Closing Disclosure three business days before consummation?
notes.back: B) The lender adds a prepayment penalty.
notes.explanation: Adding a prepayment penalty is one of the three changes that require a new waiting period.
notes.evidence: (C) A prepayment penalty is added
notes.choices:
A) The recording fee rises by $40
B) The lender adds a prepayment penalty
C) The seller agrees to pay the survey fee
notes.choicesExplained: A and C: these are ordinary changes, corrected at or before consummation without a new waiting period.

notes.front: A lender adds a $75 "document preparation" charge to settlement costs for producing the Closing Disclosure. Is this allowed?
notes.back: B) No: no fee may be imposed for preparing or delivering the Closing Disclosure.
notes.explanation: The ban applies whether the charge is part of settlement costs or collected some other way.
notes.evidence: No fee may be imposed on any person, as a part of settlement costs or otherwise, by a creditor or by a servicer
notes.choices:
A) Yes, if it is disclosed on the Loan Estimate
B) No: no fee may be imposed for preparing or delivering the Closing Disclosure
C) Yes, if the seller pays it
notes.choicesExplained: A: disclosure does not cure a prohibited fee. C: the rule bars a fee on any person, so a seller-paid fee is also barred.

notes.front: By when must the creditor deliver or post the special information booklet?
notes.back: No later than three business days after it receives the application.
notes.explanation: The clock is the same three business days used for the Loan Estimate.
notes.evidence: The creditor shall deliver or place in the mail the special information booklet not later than three business days after the consumer's application is received.

notes.front: If the consumer uses a mortgage broker, who provides the special information booklet?
notes.back: The mortgage broker; the creditor need not.
notes.explanation: One booklet is enough: when the broker provides it, the creditor is relieved of the duty.
notes.evidence: If a consumer uses a mortgage broker, the mortgage broker shall provide the special information booklet and the creditor need not do so.

notes.front: What are two kinds of transaction for which the special information booklet need not be given?
notes.back: Refinancing transactions and reverse mortgages (closed-end subordinate-lien loans too, among others).
notes.explanation: The booklet is aimed at purchases of one-to-four family homes; the list of exempt transactions is not closed.
notes.evidence: The creditor or mortgage broker need not provide the booklet to the consumer for a transaction, the purpose of which is not the purchase of a one-to-four family residential property, including, but not limited to, the following:

notes.front: For which application must the creditor provide the special information booklet?
notes.back: A) A first-time buyer's loan to purchase a single-family home
notes.explanation: The booklet is for purchases of one-to-four family residential property.
notes.evidence: the purpose of which is not the purchase of a one-to-four family residential property
notes.choices:
A) A first-time buyer's loan to purchase a single-family home
B) A refinance of an existing mortgage
C) A reverse mortgage
notes.choicesExplained: B and C: refinancing transactions and reverse mortgages are listed as not requiring the booklet.

notes.front: What must a consumer give the creditor to waive a TRID waiting period for a financial emergency?
notes.back: A dated written statement describing the emergency and waiving the period, signed by every consumer primarily liable.
notes.explanation: Printed waiver forms are prohibited, so the statement must be the consumer's own.
notes.evidence: the consumer shall give the creditor a dated written statement that describes the emergency, specifically modifies or waives the waiting period, and bears the signature of all consumers who are primarily liable on the legal obligation. Printed forms for this purpose are prohibited.

notes.front: When can the consumer waive the three-business-day Closing Disclosure waiting period?
notes.back: Only after the creditor has provided the Closing Disclosure.
notes.explanation: A waiver signed in advance, before the disclosure exists, does not work.
notes.evidence: A consumer may modify or waive the right to the three-business-day waiting periods required by § 1026.19(f)(1)(ii)(A) or (f)(2)(ii) only after the creditor makes the disclosures required by § 1026.19(f)(1)(i).

notes.front: What statement accompanies the Calculating Cash to Close table on the Closing Disclosure?
notes.back: "Use this table to see what has changed from your Loan Estimate."
notes.explanation: It is where the consumer checks the closing figures against the earlier estimate.
notes.evidence: In a separate table, under the heading “Calculating Cash to Close,” together with the statement “Use this table to see what has changed from your Loan Estimate”:

notes.front: A buyer wants to know how much money to bring on closing day. Which figure on the Closing Disclosure should she look at?
notes.back: B) Cash to Close
notes.explanation: Cash to close is the total cash or other funds the consumer must provide at consummation.
notes.evidence: the total amount of cash or other funds that must be provided by the consumer at consummation
notes.choices:
A) Loan Amount
B) Cash to Close
C) Monthly Principal & Interest
notes.choicesExplained: A: the loan amount is what she borrows, not what she brings. C: that is the regular payment after closing.

notes.front: How do the three-day rules for the Loan Estimate and the Closing Disclosure differ?
notes.back: The Loan Estimate is delivered or posted within three business days after application; the Closing Disclosure must be received three business days before consummation.
notes.explanation: One counts forward from the application and turns on sending; the other counts back from closing and turns on receipt.
notes.source: CFPB, TILA-RESPA Integrated Disclosure: Guide to the Loan Estimate and Closing Disclosure forms (v2.1), 1. Introduction, p. 8
notes.evidence: Consumers must receive the Closing Disclosure no later than three business days before consummation of their loan.

notes.front: A lender still hands applicants one set of disclosure forms under the Truth in Lending Act and another under RESPA for a closed-end home purchase loan. What has it missed?
notes.back: A) The TRID rule replaced those with the Loan Estimate and the Closing Disclosure.
notes.explanation: The Bureau issued integrated disclosures so that one form is given early and one before closing.
notes.source: CFPB, TILA-RESPA Integrated Disclosure: Guide to the Loan Estimate and Closing Disclosure forms (v2.1), 1. Introduction, p. 7
notes.evidence: On December 31, 2013, the Bureau published a final rule with new, integrated disclosures
notes.choices:
A) The TRID rule replaced those with the Loan Estimate and the Closing Disclosure
B) Nothing: both sets are still required
C) Only that the forms must be sent by email
notes.choicesExplained: B: the integrated forms replaced the separate ones for these loans. C: delivery method is not the issue.

notes.front: How do zero tolerance, 10 percent tolerance and the no-limit category differ?
notes.back: Zero: no increase. 10 percent: category total may rise up to 10 per cent. No limit: any change if the estimate used the best information.
notes.explanation: Zero tolerance is the general rule; the other two categories are the exceptions the regulation sets out.
notes.evidence: regardless of whether the amount paid by the consumer exceeds the amount disclosed under paragraph (e)(1)(i) of this section.

notes.front: When does a creditor use a revised Loan Estimate rather than a corrected Closing Disclosure?
notes.back: A revised Loan Estimate only before the Closing Disclosure is provided; from that day on, a corrected Closing Disclosure.
notes.explanation: The revised Loan Estimate must also reach the consumer at least four business days before consummation.
notes.evidence: The consumer must receive any revised version of the disclosures required under paragraph (e)(1)(i) of this section not later than four business days prior to consummation.

notes.front: What are the two meanings of business day in TRID timing?
notes.back: Offices open for substantially all functions (Loan Estimate delivery); all days except Sundays and legal public holidays (waiting periods).
notes.explanation: Which one applies depends on the timing rule being counted.
notes.evidence: the term “business day” means all calendar days except Sundays and legal public holidays
